newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Bank may alter MGAM control.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Bank may alter MGAM control.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG said on Tuesday a decision to send a German manager into London-based Morgan Grenfell was linked to a possible switch of management reporting lines for the unit trust business to Frankfurt.

A Deutsche spokesman said the bank had long considered putting its British trust business under Frankfurt's supervision, but problems at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) had given the idea new impetus.
He stressed that Deutsche was considering shifting reporting lines, not the management of the funds themselves.

MGAM last week temporarily suspended trading in three of its European funds due to suspected irregularities. The affair has embarrassed Deutsche and rattled confidence in unit trusts, hitherto seen as a safe home for an investor.

The furore has also hit Deutsche's share price. Rumours of a shakeout at top management levels -- described by the bank as "utter nonsense" -- helped to send its shares down 39 pfennigs to 71.50 marks in a rising market on Tuesday.

The manager of two of the troubled MGAM funds, Peter Young, has been suspended and his assets frozen pending a probe into the management of the trusts, which held a high proportion of speculative, unlisted, high-technology stocks.
Deutsche last week took these stocks into its books in return for a 180 million pound ($279.7 million) cash injection into MGAM.
A German small shareholder protection group on Tuesday attacked Deutsche for a "catastrophic" blow to the bank's image caysed by the scandal and predicted shareholders would bear the brunt.
"This was a total failure of internal controls," Reinhild Keitel, a director of the SdK group, told German radio.
"For several years we have been thinking about managing the fund business for private clients from Frankfurt," Deutsche spokesman Hellmut Hartmann told Reuters.
"After the problems in London these considerations have been renewed and it could well be that this will happen but no decision has been taken yet.
"In this context we have sent one of our fund managers to London to act as an adviser for measures being taken there."
Management supervision for Morgan Grenfell's institutional fund business would remain in London, Hartmann said.
Analysts said a switch of management responsibility from London to Frankfurt would be a logical consequence of Deutsche's reorganisation announced in July.

Under that revamp, Deutsche created a division called Private Customers, run by board members Georg Krupp and Tessin von Heydebreck, which included private asset management. But Morgan Grenfell's unit trust business remained allocated to a separate division, Investment Banking. That may now change.
Deutsche has appointed Udo Behrenwaldt, a managing director of its German investment subsidiary DWS Deutsche Gesellschaft fuer Wertpapiersparen mbH, as an adviser to MGAM in London.

That is the first step towards stricter management supervision from Frankfurt since Deutsche's head of global fund management, Rolf Breuer, last week announced an overhaul of internal controls at MGAM.

Hartmann reiterated that Deutsche Morgan Grenfell would pay compensation if the current investigation by the British fund industry watchdog, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO), found it was liable.

Konrad Becker, an analyst at Merck, Finck in Frankfurt, said he had lowered his 1996 earnings-per-share forecast for Deutsche to 4.50 marks from five marks to account for the cash injection and possible compensation payments. ($1=.6436 Pound)
